questions.q: What was the Permanent Settlement, and what were its consequences?

answer.text: The Permanent Settlement was introduced in Bengal in 1793 by Lord Cornwallis. Under it the zamindars were recognised as the proprietors of land and were required to pay a fixed amount of revenue to the Company, which would never be increased. The aim was to secure a steady income and to create a loyal, improving class of landlords.

The results, however, were harsh. The revenue was fixed so high that many zamindars could not pay, and under the sunset law their estates were auctioned if payment was late, so many lost their lands. A new group of rich peasants, the jotedars, rose in the villages. Above all, the actual cultivators, the raiyats, were squeezed for rent and gained little protection.

answer: Thus the Permanent Settlement disrupted rural society and burdened the peasantry, while failing in its aim of prosperity.

questions.q: Why did the Deccan ryots revolt in 1875?
answer: The Deccan riots of 1875 were an uprising of peasants, or ryots, in the Bombay Deccan against the moneylenders on whom they depended.

answer.text: During the American Civil War, cotton exports from India rose sharply and prices boomed, and ryots borrowed freely to grow more cotton. When the war ended, demand and prices collapsed, but the ryots' debts remained.

The revenue demand under the ryotwari system was high and inflexible, and to pay it the ryots fell ever deeper into the hands of moneylenders, who charged heavy interest and seized their land and property through the courts.
Enraged by this exploitation, the ryots attacked the moneylenders and burnt the bonds and deeds that recorded their debts, prompting the government to appoint the Deccan Riots Commission.

answer: Thus rural debt and colonial revenue policy drove the peasants to revolt.
